inline.s: [The Aspiration to Be Born in the West] This is the Pure Land aspiration text composed by Master Lianchi, the Eighth Patriarch of the Pure Land school and an eminent monk of the Ming Dynasty, aspiring to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. There are many kinds of Pure Land aspiration texts, but only this one is complete in both principle and practice and is the most perfect and wondrous. Therefore Master Xing'an (the Eleventh Patriarch of the Pure Land school) said: "Other texts (other Pure Land aspiration texts) may be followed and revered, yet their wording and meaning are not complete; this aspiration text alone is complete in meaning and wording." He also said: "This aspiration text is complete in principle and practice, and its practice and vows are profound and vast. All who have wisdom should savor its words and strive to put them into practice, so that both self and others may benefit and both cause and effect be fulfilled, and not merely chant the words and sounds in chorus." (Annotations on the Aspiration to Be Born in the West)
[Master Lianchi] (

) An eminent monk of the Ming Dynasty. His secular surname was Shen, his given name Zhuhong, and his sobriquet Lianchi. He cultivated the samadhi of Buddha-recitation with great diligence and strove to expound the dual practice of Chan and Pure Land. He dwelt on Mount Yunqi in Hangzhou, and so was also known as Master Yunqi. He was the Eighth Patriarch of the Pure Land school. Throughout his life he cultivated the Pure Land with devotion and spread its teachings widely. Half a month before his death he knew in advance that his time had come. He went into the city to take leave of his disciples and old friends, saying only: "I am going elsewhere." Returning to the monastery, he offered tea to the assembled monks and told them he would set out the next day. On the evening of the first day of the seventh month, Master Lianchi showed a slight illness and sat with closed eyes and no words. When his disciples from the city arrived and tearfully begged him to leave final instructions, Master Lianchi opened his eyes and said: "Recite the Buddha's name honestly; do not change the subject." Having spoken, he faced west, called the Buddha's name, and passed away. He lived eighty-one years and had fifty years of monastic seniority. His writings are abundant; the chief among those in circulation are the Commentary and Notes on the Amitabha Sutra, the Yunqi Dharma Collection, Casual Writings from the Bamboo Window, Records of Rebirth, and Clearing Doubts about the Pure Land.

[Master Xing'an] (1686-1734) A native of Changshu in Jiangsu. His monastic name was Shixian, his courtesy name Siqi, and his sobriquet Xing'an. He was an eminent monk of the Qing Dynasty and the Eleventh Patriarch of the Pure Land school. Because he awakened through investigating the question "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?", from then on his Dharma combat was swift and sharp and his eloquence unbridled. Later, at Fantian Temple, he devoted himself solely to the Pure Land. In his later years he held to the Buddha's name; he burned a finger before the Buddha at Mount Ayuwang, made forty-eight great vows, and moved the relics to emit light. He composed An Essay Urging the Giving Rise to the Bodhi Mind to inspire the four assemblies, and many who recited it shed tears. On the Buddha's Enlightenment Day in the eleventh year of Yongzheng (1733), he told his disciples: "I shall depart on the fourteenth day of the fourth month next year." Having said this, he entered retreat to recite the Buddha's name, with a daily fixed practice of one hundred thousand recitations. On the twelfth day of the fourth month the following year he left retreat and gave instructions to his disciples. When an attendant asked the Master to leave a verse, he wrote: "The body amid flowers, the Buddha appears before me; / Buddha-light shines upon the purple golden lotus; / The mind follows all Buddhas to rebirth; / In neither coming nor going, the matter is just so." Having written it, he said: "On the fourteenth I shall certainly be reborn." On the thirteenth he sat cross-legged in silent meditation, and at the fifth watch he rose and bathed. At the hour of Si on the fourteenth, he said to his disciples: "You must take the great matter of birth and death to heart and recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly." Having spoken, he joined his palms and faced west, and amid the sound of Buddha-recitation was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[The Buddha's Enlightenment Day] The day of the Buddha's enlightenment. The Buddha's descent and birth, his enlightenment, and his parinirvana all fall on the full-moon day of May in the solar calendar.

This text can be divided into seven chapters: 1. Giving rise to the bodhi mind, 2. Repenting of the three obstructions, 3. Making the four great vows, 4. Seeking birth in the Pure Land, 5. Returning to the Saha world, 6. Stating the great vows in full, 7. Dedicating the merit to all beings. These seven chapters encompass without omission the whole sequence of Pure Land practice, from the first arousal of the aspiration to the universal deliverance of all beings.

blocks.text: The Aspiration to Be Born in the West (Original Text)

inline.s: by Master Lianchi
I bow my head to the Land of Bliss in the West, / Great guiding teacher, who leads all beings to rest.
I now make vows, for rebirth I aspire; / I pray your compassion will grant my desire.

I, disciple (so-and-so), for the sake of the four kinds of kindness, the three existences, and all beings of the dharma-realm, seeking the One Vehicle, the unsurpassed bodhi path of all Buddhas, single-mindedly hold and recite the myriad-virtue great name of Amitabha Buddha, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land. And because my karma is heavy and my merit light, my obstructions deep and my wisdom shallow, the defiled mind easily blazes while pure virtue is hard to accomplish. Now before the Buddha I bow with all five limbs in earnest, laying bare my whole heart, and take refuge in repentance.

I and all beings, from distant kalpas until now, have lost our original pure mind and given free rein to greed, anger, and delusion. The defiled three karmas are immeasurable and boundless; the offenses and defilements committed are immeasurable and boundless; the enmities bound up, may they all be wiped away. From this day on I make profound vows: to keep far from evil dharmas and vow never to create them again; to diligently cultivate the noble path and vow never to retreat or grow lazy; to vow to attain perfect enlightenment; to vow to save all beings. Amitabha Buddha, by the power of your compassionate vows, will surely bear witness to me, take pity on me, and bless me. May I, in meditation and contemplation and in dreams and sleep, see the golden body of Amitabha Buddha, visit the jewel-adorned land of Amitabha Buddha, receive the sweet dew poured upon my crown by Amitabha Buddha, have his light shine upon my body, his hand stroke my head, his robe cover my body. May my past obstructions be removed of themselves and my roots of goodness grow. May afflictions be swiftly emptied and ignorance suddenly shattered. May the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment open wide in awakening. May the true realm of tranquil light ever be present before me.

As for the time when death approaches, may I know the hour in advance. May my body be free of all sickness, suffering, and calamity, and my mind free of all attachment and confusion. May my faculties be joyful and my right mindfulness clear. May I relinquish the reward in peace, as if entering samadhi. May Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and the hosts of noble sages, send forth light to receive me and reach down their hands to lift me up. May pavilions and banners, rare fragrances and heavenly music, and the holy scenes of the West be shown before my eyes. May all beings who see or hear of it rejoice and sigh in admiration and give rise to the bodhi mind.

At that time I shall ride upon a diamond platform, following behind the Buddha; in the time of a finger-snap I shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, within a victory lotus in a pool of seven jewels. The flower will open and I shall see the Buddha and behold the bodhisattvas, hear the wondrous Dharma sound, and attain the patient acceptance of non-arising. In an instant I shall serve all Buddhas and personally receive their predictions. Having received the predictions, the three bodies and four wisdoms, the five eyes and six spiritual powers, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharanis, all merits and virtues, shall be perfected. Then, without abandoning the Land of Peace and Nurture, I shall return to the Saha world. Multiplying my body without number, I shall fill the lands of the ten directions. By inconceivable, sovereign spiritual power and various skillful means, I shall liberate all beings. I shall cause them all to be free of defilement and regain the pure mind. Together may we be born in the West and enter the stage of non-retrogression.

Vows such as these: as worlds are endless, beings are endless, and karma and afflictions are all endless, so are my vows endless. May the merit of today's worshipping the Buddha, making vows, and cultivating practice be dedicated to all sentient beings. May the four kinds of kindness be universally repaid and the three existences alike be benefited. May all beings of the dharma-realm together perfect the wisdom of the Buddha.
[I bow my head to the Land of Bliss in the West, / Great guiding teacher, who leads all beings to rest. / I now make vows, for rebirth I aspire; / I pray your compassion will grant my desire.]

In this verse, the first two lines take refuge in Amitabha Buddha, the great guiding teacher who receives all beings into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the last two lines are the vow to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and a prayer for Amitabha Buddha's blessing and protection.

[Bowing the head] To touch the head to the ground, pause for a moment, and then rise; hence it is called "bowing the head," expressing the utmost reverence. [The Western Land of Peace and Bliss] That is, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Great guiding teacher] Here it refers to Amitabha Buddha. [Making vows] To utter solemn vows before the Buddha. Once the one who makes the vow has uttered this solemn vow, it becomes the guiding principle of his thought and conduct, and body, speech, and mind must follow it and strive earnestly to fulfill it.

blocks.text: 1. Giving Rise to the Bodhi Mind

inline.s: In cultivating the Pure Land teaching, the most important thing is to have the bodhi mind that benefits both self and others. Without giving rise to the bodhi mind, one cannot be born in the Pure Land; hence the aspiration text begins with giving rise to the bodhi mind. In the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says: "Those who wish to be born in that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) should cultivate three blessings. First, to support and care for one's parents, to serve and attend one's teachers, to be compassionate and refrain from killing, and to cultivate the ten wholesome actions. Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to keep the precepts in full, and not to violate the rules of deportment. Third, to give rise to the bodhi mind, to deeply believe in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahayana scriptures, and to encourage others to advance."

Master Xing'an's An Essay Urging the Giving Rise to the Bodhi Mind says: "The essential gate of entering the path is the arousal of the aspiration; the urgent task of practice is the making of vows first. When vows are made, beings can be saved; when the mind is aroused, the Buddha path can be accomplished. If one does not arouse the vast mind and make firm vows, then though kalpas as numerous as dust pass by, one still remains in samsara; though one practices, it is all vain toil and hardship. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'To forget and lose the bodhi mind while cultivating wholesome dharmas is the work of Mara.' If forgetting is already so, how much more so when one has never aroused it? Thus we know that one who wishes to study the Tathagata's vehicle must first fully arouse the bodhisattva's vow; there is no room for delay."

Master Chewu said: "The sixteen characters 'truly for the sake of birth and death, give rise to the bodhi mind, with deep faith and vows, hold the Buddha's name' are the great guiding principle of the Buddha-recitation gate." "Now, I have birth and death and seek liberation. Yet all beings are likewise in birth and death and all should be liberated. They and I are originally of one body, all former parents and future Buddhas. If one does not think of universal deliverance but seeks only self-benefit, then principle is deficient and the mind uneasy. Moreover, if the great mind (the bodhi mind) is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot resonate with all Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with one's own nature; above, one cannot perfect the Buddha path, and below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitude. How shall beginningless affection be untied? How shall beginningless grievances be resolved? Offenses accumulated over kalpas are hard to expiate; roots of goodness accumulated over kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. In whatever practice one undertakes, obstacles and conditions abound. Even if something is accomplished, in the end one falls into partiality and the lesser vehicle. Therefore one must arouse the great bodhi mind in accordance with one's nature." (The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)

Peng Jiqing's Preface to the Posthumous Writings of Master Xing'an says: "Formerly, when our World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he sighed: 'How strange! How strange! Not one being is without the Tathagata's wisdom, yet because of delusive thought, inversion, and attachment they cannot realize it. If they were free of delusive thought, then all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom would appear before them.' I have never understood why these beings, amid delusive thought and attachment, do not trouble to be free of them, and with regard to the Tathagata's wisdom, what they fear in realizing it. In the end they abandon the father and flee away, drifting for long kalpas, willing to be hired servants and base men, and never knowing to turn back. There is no other reason: they are simply unaware. The bodhi mind is but another name for awareness. As soon as one is aware, the delusive thought and attachment before one are entirely the Tathagata's wisdom. For the Tathagata's wisdom has no substance of its own; it takes the beings' delusive thought as its substance. The beings' delusive thought has no substance of its own; it takes the Tathagata's wisdom as its substance. It is like water becoming waves: the whole wave is water. From the very beginning, one is ultimately to abide in nirvana without residue. Yet the distinction between awareness and unawareness can never be concealed or obscured from oneself. If one thinks on this with a start and understands with a crack, then the arousing of the bodhi mind will of itself be surging and irresistible. Once this mind is aroused, all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom appear before one; what need is there to seek elsewhere?"

[All-wisdom, natural wisdom, unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom of the Buddha. [Like water becoming waves: the whole wave is water] Still water (water) and moving water (waves) are one body in two states (two states of the same thing). When still water is agitated it becomes moving water and has waves; when the waves subside, moving water turns back into still water. [Cracking sound] An onomatopoeic word, often used to describe the sound of breaking, snapping, or opening.
[Master Chewu] (

) A monk of the Qing Dynasty. His secular surname was Ma, his given name Jixing, and his courtesy name Chewu. He was the Thirty-sixth Patriarch of the Linji school and the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, thoroughly versed in the Chan school, the teachings, and the Pure Land. The Master often recalled Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, a master craftsman of the Chan gate, who still turned his heart to the Pure Land and daily recited the Buddha's name one hundred thousand times, aspiring to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; moreover, in this Dharma-ending age one should all the more follow Chan Master Yongming's legacy. So he settled his mind in the Pure Land and upheld the Lotus school. Each day he set aside only the time it takes to burn one stick of incense for receiving visitors; all the rest was spent bowing to the Buddha and reciting his name. The Master deeply grasped the profound purport of both the Chan and Pure Land schools. He was strict with himself and earnest with others; in expounding and teaching the Dharma he poured it out like a bottle, like clouds rising, and was at that time the foremost man of the Dharma gate. Whenever he expounded the Tathagata's grace of saving from suffering and giving joy, the Master would weep as he spoke, and none of his listeners failed to shed tears that wet their clothes. Master Yongming said, 'To have Chan and have Pure Land is like a horned tiger: in this life one is a teacher of men, in the next one becomes a Buddha or a Patriarch' - this is seen here. The Master knew his time in advance. In the second month of the fifteenth year of Jiaqing he went to Wanshou Temple to sweep the ancestral stupa and take leave of the mountain's lay protectors. In the third month he returned to the mountain and ordered preparations for his cremation. On the seventeenth day of the tenth month he assembled the assembly and handed over the affairs of the monastery, instructing his disciple Songquan to lead the assembly. Half a month before his manifest passing, he saw in empty space countless banners coming from the west. He told the assembly: "The marks of the Pure Land have appeared; I shall return to the West." The assembly urged him to remain in the world, and the Master said: "A hundred years are but a lodging; in the end there is somewhere to return to. I have attained the holy realm; you should rejoice for me - why trouble to keep me?" On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month he ordered a nirvana feast to be prepared. At the hour of Shen (three in the afternoon) on the seventeenth, he told the assembly: "Yesterday I already saw the three great beings Manjusri, Avalokitesvara, and Mahasthamaprapta; now I have again received the Buddha's own descent to receive me. I go now." The assembly recited the Buddha's name all the more earnestly, and the Master, sitting upright facing west with joined palms, said: "Recite one sound of the great name, see one share of the marks of excellence." Then he formed the Amitabha mudra with his hands and passed away in peace; the assembly smelled rare fragrance floating in the air. He was enshrined for seven days with a countenance as if alive, kindly and full, his white hair turned black and unusually lustrous. On the second seventh day he was placed in the coffin, and on the third seventh day cremated; more than a hundred relics were obtained.
[Peng Jiqing] (1740-1796

) His name was Shaosheng, his courtesy name Yunchu, his sobriquet Chimu, also known as Zhiguizi and the layman Erlin; Jiqing was the Dharma name he received on taking the bodhisattva precepts. He was born into a typical scholarly family in Changzhou County, Jiangsu (present-day Suzhou). As a child he was already bright and wise. At sixteen he passed the county examination as a xiucai; the next year he passed the provincial examination as a juren; the third year he passed the metropolitan examination in the capital as a jinshi, and with the renown of a jinshi he lived out his days at home. He was by nature extremely filial: during his mother's mourning he guarded her grave for three years. When his father passed away, he established a Buddha-recitation hall for him and vowed to dedicate to his father's rebirth in the Western Pure Land the merit of ten recitations of the Avatamsaka Sutra, one thousand recitations of the Amitabha Sutra, one thousand recitations of the Diamond Sutra, and ten million recitations of the Buddha's name, all of which he had recited in daily practice. Later he entirely abandoned the learning he had previously pursued and devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures, composing A Treatise Resolving Doubts about the One Vehicle to bridge the barrier between Confucianism and Buddhism. He also wrote A Treatise on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi of the Avatamsaka to settle the dispute between the Chan and Pure Land schools, and A New Treatise on the Three Pure Land Sutras to expound fully the meaning that the earlier Pure Land school had not entirely made clear. His compiled Biographies of Lay Buddhists, Biographies of Virtuous Women, and Records of Pure Land Sages and Worthies guided beings according to their capacities and were widely circulated and recited in the world. He also once raised ten thousand taels of gold and used the interest to build temples, print scriptures, and make offerings to the monastic assembly, and he established the "Jinqu Hall" to relieve the poor and needy. He also set up the "Renze Field" to support poor clansmen. He founded the "Lixu Society" to relieve widowed women, and established the "Life-Release Society" to preserve the lives of living beings. All such good works each had its own aspiration text, and all were dedicated to rebirth together in the Western Pure Land. Later, in the monasteries of the Suzhou and Hangzhou region, he lived in seclusion and practiced for more than ten years, with a fixed daily course. He himself arranged beforehand the matters of his death and burial and had it that no heir need be established for him (since he had only daughters). In the sixtieth year of Qianlong (1795

) in the autumn he contracted dysentery, and after the beginning of winter his spirits gradually declined. He handed over the funds of the various charitable societies one by one to his nephew Peng Zhuhua, instructing him to carry them on and not let these good works be interrupted. At that time a monk named Zhenqing asked him whether he had ever seen auspicious signs or responses. Peng Jiqing said: "What auspicious signs! My great matter is on the day the government offices open in the first month of next year!" On the morning of the twentieth day of the first month of the first year of Jiaqing (1796

) he composed a farewell verse: "A speck of dust-body appearing and vanishing in Jambudvipa, / Drifting and straggling, for what cause at all? / Now I go straight to the West; / A blink reclaims ten thousand kalpas of spring." Then, facing west, he sat upright and, holding the Buddha's name, was peacefully liberated. It was indeed the very day the government offices opened at the start of that year. He was fifty-seven years old.

[I, disciple (so-and-so), for the sake of the four kinds of kindness, the three existences, and all beings of the dharma-realm, seeking the One Vehicle, the unsurpassed bodhi path of all Buddhas, single-mindedly hold and recite the myriad-virtue great name of Amitabha Buddha, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land.]

I, disciple so-and-so, in order to universally save the beings of the four kinds of kindness, the beings of the three realms, and indeed the beings of the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, and for the sake of seeking the One Vehicle, the unsurpassed bodhi path of all Buddhas, single-mindedly hold and recite the myriad-virtue great name of Amitabha Buddha, and will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Giving rise to the bodhi mind] To arouse the great mind that seeks the Buddha path above (to become a Buddha) and transforms beings below. [So-and-so] A pronoun for referring to oneself. When reciting, one should replace the words "so-and-so" with one's own name. [The four kinds of kindness] The kindness of parents (family), the kindness of beings (society), the kindness of the land (nation), and the kindness of the Three Jewels (the Buddhist gate). [The Three Jewels] The Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel. All Buddhas are the Buddha Jewel; the Dharma taught by the Buddha is the Dharma Jewel; those who practice the Dharma taught by the Buddha are the Sangha Jewel. Buddha means awareness and knowing; Dharma means the norm and model; Sangha means harmony.

[The three existences] The three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. (Note: "the three existences" also refers to birth and death within the three realms. Birth and death in the three realms have cause and effect, and so are called "the three existences." First, the existence of desire, that is, birth and death in the realm of desire; second, the existence of form, that is, birth and death in the realm of form; third, the formless existence, that is, birth and death in the formless realm. Here "the three existences" should mean the three realms. Master Xing'an's Annotations on the Aspiration to Be Born in the West says: "As for the words 'three existences,' they are the three realms, namely the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.")

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sex and food; it extends from the six heavens of desire above, through the world of humans and animals in the middle, down to the uninterrupted hell below. The realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still have form; the four dhyanas and eighteen heavens belong to it. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who are entirely without form but abide with mind-consciousness in profound and wondrous samadhi; the four formless heavens belong to it. These three realms are all the territory in which ordinary beings come and go through birth and death, and so the practitioner's aim is to leap out of the three realms. [Beings of the dharma-realm] All beings of the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.

[One Vehicle] Also called the Buddha Vehicle, the only teaching that can lead people to Buddhahood. "Vehicle" means a carriage, used to illustrate the Buddha's teaching: the teaching can carry people across to the other shore of nirvana, and so is called a "vehicle." [Unsurpassed bodhi path] The path to Buddhahood. [Single-mindedly holding and reciting] Calling the Buddha's name with one whole heart and mind. [Aspiring to be born in the Pure Land] Certainly to be born in the Pure Land; "aspiring" here means "certainly, definitely."

blocks.text: 2. Repenting and Removing the Three Obstructions

inline.s: This passage connects with the preceding text. Although one has previously established the unsurpassed bodhi vow and recites the Buddha's name seeking birth in the Pure Land, if one is obstructed by afflictions, evil karma, and evil retribution, pure virtue is hard to accomplish; how then can one attain birth? So the pressing task is to repent of and remove the three obstructions.

[The three obstructions] The obstruction of afflictions, the obstruction of karma, and the obstruction of retribution. The obstruction of afflictions is the obstruction caused by afflictions; the obstruction of karma is the obstruction caused by committed evil karma; the obstruction of retribution is the obstruction caused by evil retribution manifesting.
This passage clarifies the cause of repentance.
[And because my karma is heavy and my merit light, my obstructions deep and my wisdom shallow, the defiled mind easily blazes while pure virtue is hard to accomplish.]

Yet because one's own karma is heavy and one's merit light, and because the three obstructions are deep and wisdom shallow, the defiled mind easily blazes while the virtue of pure practice is hard to accomplish.
This passage clarifies the method of repentance.
[Now before the Buddha, bowing with all five limbs in earnest, laying bare my whole heart, I take refuge in repentance:]
Now before the Buddha, earnestly longing for Amitabha Buddha's compassionate blessing (protection), I, your disciple, lay bare my heart and weep blood, and repent in utmost sincerity:

[Earnest longing] Also written as "qiaoqin," to long for earnestly. [Five limbs] The four limbs and the head, meaning the whole body. [Laying bare] To lay bare one's liver and drip one's gall, that is, to be utterly sincere. [Taking refuge] To offer up a sincere heart. [Repentance] To repent (chan) means to blame oneself for the past; to regret (hui) means to resolutely cut off the future.
This passage formally sets forth the repentance.

[I and all beings, from distant kalpas until now, have lost our original pure mind and given free rein to greed, anger, and delusion; the defiled three karmas are immeasurable and boundless; the offenses and defilements committed are immeasurable and boundless; the enmities bound up
(immeasurable and boundless)
, may they all be wiped away.]

I and all beings, since beginningless kalpas, have lost our own originally pure mind and so have given free rein to the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion. From this we have created the defiled three karmas of body, speech, and mind, immeasurable and boundless; the evil mental defilements thereby produced are likewise immeasurable and boundless; and the enmities thereby bound up with beings are likewise immeasurable and boundless. May they all be entirely wiped away.

[Distant kalpas] The very distant past is called "distant kalpas"; the very distant future is called "eternal kalpas." [The three poisons] Greed, anger, and delusion. Greed is craving for the five desires; anger is wrath without forbearance; delusion is folly and ignorance. Because greed, anger, and delusion can poison people's physical life and wisdom life, they are called the "three poisons," and they are also the root of all afflictions. [The five desires] Forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects. "Form" means beautiful appearances; "sound" means pleasing sounds and delightful speech; "fragrance" means fragrant scents; "taste" means delicious flavors; "touch" means agreeable tactile pleasure. Because these five can cause people to give rise to a mind of craving, they are called the five desires. To keep the precepts purely means being able to control the five faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) and not be moved by the five desires. In the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, when the Buddha taught the key to keeping the precepts, he said: "One should restrain the five faculties and not let them run loose into the five desires. It is like a cowherd holding a staff and watching the cattle, not letting them wander and trample others' sprouts and crops." [The three karmas] Karma of body, karma of speech, and karma of mind.

[The enmities bound up] Before the four characters "the enmities bound up" come "the defiled three karmas are immeasurable and boundless, the offenses and defilements committed are immeasurable and boundless," and after them comes "may they all be wiped away." Judging from the sense of the text, it seems it should read "the enmities bound up are immeasurable and boundless," that is: "the defiled three karmas are immeasurable and boundless, the offenses and defilements committed are immeasurable and boundless, the enmities bound up are immeasurable and boundless; may they all be wiped away." The appearance of this situation may be an omission in the course of copying and transmission. The Master's original text must not be altered at will; I have respectfully supplied the four characters "immeasurable and boundless" in parentheses, to seek instruction from the great virtuous ones of all quarters.
A verse says:
For all the evil karma wrought in days gone by, / Born of beginningless greed, anger, and folly,
Springing from body, speech, and mind, / All of it I now repent.
Another verse says:
Offenses rise up from the mind; with the mind I repent them. / When the mind is extinguished, offenses too are gone;
Mind extinguished, offenses gone, both are empty; / This alone is called true repentance.

Now that the afflictions and delusions in the mind have been entirely purified and past evil karma has also been wiped away, if one's vows are not firm, one will still unavoidably retreat and grow lazy in practice. Therefore one should again make the four great vows, to restrain one's own mind and ensure the fulfillment of the great vows previously made.

[From this day on, I make profound vows: to keep far from evil dharmas and vow never to create them again; to diligently cultivate the noble path and vow never to retreat or grow lazy; to vow to attain perfect enlightenment; to vow to save all beings.]

From this day on, I make profound and vast vows: to keep far from all evil dharmas and vow never again to create them; to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed Buddha path and vow never to retreat or grow lazy; to vow to accomplish unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; to vow to universally save all beings of the dharma-realm.

[The noble path] The path of the noble ones; here it means the One Vehicle, the unsurpassed bodhi path. [Vowing to attain perfect enlightenment] Vowing to accomplish unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, that is, to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

Master Xing'an's Annotations on the Aspiration to Be Born in the West says: "These are the four great vows. If practice has no vows, there will be regression and loss; hence these four dharmas restrain one's own mind so that laziness does not arise. ... Here it says to keep far from evil dharmas and vow never to create them again, which is 'afflictions are endless, I vow to cut them off' - this arouses the mind based on the truth of origin. To diligently cultivate the noble path and vow never to retreat or grow lazy is 'the Dharma gates are measureless, I vow to learn them' - this arouses the mind based on the truth of the path. To vow to attain perfect enlightenment is 'the Buddha path is unsurpassed, I vow to accomplish it' - this arouses the mind based on the truth of cessation. To vow to save all beings is 'beings are boundless, I vow to save them' - this arouses the mind based on the truth of suffering. Though the order of the words differs, the meaning is not two."

[The four great vows] Also called the "four vast vows." All Buddhas have general vows and particular vows; the four great vows are the general vows, and when all bodhisattvas first arouse the mind they must make these vows. Because what is aspired to is vast and universal it is called "great"; because it restrains one's own mind it is called an "oath"; because one resolves to fulfill it, it is called an "aspiration." These four vows are made in dependence on the Four Noble Truths (suffering, origin, cessation, and path). The Essentials of Calming and Contemplation states: First, "beings are boundless, I vow to save them" - this is the vow to save boundless beings in dependence on the truth of suffering. Second, "afflictions are numberless, I vow to cut them off" - this is the vow to cut off endless afflictions in dependence on the truth of origin. Third, "the Dharma gates are endless, I vow to learn them" - this is the vow to learn endless Dharma gates in dependence on the truth of the path. Fourth, "the Buddha path is unsurpassed, I vow to accomplish it" - this is the vow to accomplish the endless Buddha path in dependence on the truth of cessation. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind Ground says: "All bodhisattvas further have four vows by which they bring beings to maturity and sustain the Three Jewels, never retreating to the end of the great ocean of kalpas. What are the four? First, to vow to save all beings; second, to vow to cut off all afflictions; third, to vow to learn all Dharma gates; fourth, to vow to realize all Buddha fruits."

[The Four Noble Truths] The truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and path. First, the "truth of suffering" is the truth explaining that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the reality of actual life. Second, the "origin" of the "truth of origin" means to bring about or cause; it is the truth explaining how life's suffering comes to be. Life's suffering arises because craving creates karma, and so one suffers and transmigrates. Third, the "truth of cessation" is the truth explaining the cessation of all suffering. When all the origin of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, without defilement or attachment, one no longer suffers or transmigrates; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the "truth of the path" is the truth explaining how to forever cut off the origin of suffering (craving), that is, the path of ending suffering. Among the Four Noble Truths, origin is the cause and suffering is the effect; path is the cause and cessation is the effect.

blocks.text: 4. Seeking Birth in the Pure Land

inline.s: Now that the bodhi mind and the four great vows have both been established, and afflictions and karmic obstructions have also been purified, one can cultivate Buddha-recitation to the point of single-mindedness without distraction and be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore the most important thing is to seek birth in the Pure Land; this is the central link.

[Single-mindedness without distraction] There are two levels of single-mindedness: single-mindedness in practice and single-mindedness in principle. Master Ouyi said: "Single-mindedness in practice means clear and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered; single-mindedness in principle means silently according with non-arising and clearly understanding one's own nature." (Collected Works of Lingfeng, Casual Talks from the Brahman Chamber)

[Amitabha Buddha, by the power of your compassionate vows, will surely bear witness to me, take pity on me, and bless me. May I, in meditation and contemplation and in dreams and sleep, see the golden body of Amitabha Buddha, visit the jewel-adorned land of Amitabha Buddha, receive the sweet dew poured upon my crown by Amitabha Buddha, have his light shine upon my body, his hand stroke my head, his robe cover my body. May my past obstructions be removed of themselves and my roots of goodness grow. May afflictions be swiftly emptied and ignorance suddenly shattered. May the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment open wide in awakening. May the true realm of tranquil light ever be present before me.]

Amitabha Buddha, by the power of his compassionate vows, will surely bear witness to me, take pity on me, and bless me. I pray that in meditation and contemplation and in dreams and sleep I may see the golden body of Amitabha Buddha, visit the seven-jewel-adorned land of Amitabha Buddha, receive the sweet dew poured upon my crown by Amitabha Buddha, have his light shine upon my body, his hand stroke my head, his robe cover my body. May my past obstructions be removed of themselves and my roots of goodness grow; may afflictions be swiftly emptied and ignorance suddenly shattered. May the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment open wide in awakening; may the true realm of tranquil light ever be present before me.

[Chan contemplation] That is, the sixteen contemplations of the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, beginning with the contemplation of the sun and continuing to the nine grades of rebirth. [Vast and open] Broad and empty. [Tranquil light] Refers to the two virtues of principle and wisdom. "Tranquil" is the stillness of truth; "light" is the illumination of true wisdom. The state in which this truth and true wisdom are realized is called the field of tranquil light, that is, the "true realm of tranquil light" spoken of here.
Master Xing'an's Annotations on the Aspiration to Be Born in the West says:

"Chan contemplation means the sixteen contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of the sun and continuing to the nine grades of rebirth. One may contemplate all sixteen, or devote oneself to a single contemplation. As for a single contemplation, this refers for now to the comprehensive contemplation: that is, contemplating one's own body seated within a lotus, with the thought of the lotus opening and closing; when the lotus opens, Amitabha and the hosts of sages all emit light that comes to shine upon my body, and the water, birds, and trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma; this is called the comprehensive contemplation. Or one may simply contemplate the Buddha's form, sixteen feet tall, standing upon the water of the pool, reaching down his hand to lift one up, while one's own body kneels on the lotus; this too is acceptable."

"Because the sweet dew is poured upon my crown, past obstructions are removed. Because light shines upon my body, roots of goodness grow. Because his hand strokes my head, afflictions and ignorance are suddenly shattered. Because his robe covers my body, the wondrous mind and true realm appear before me."

[As for the time when death approaches, may I know the hour in advance. May my body be free of all sickness, suffering, and calamity, and my mind free of all attachment and confusion. May my faculties be joyful and my right mindfulness clear. May I relinquish the reward in peace, as if entering samadhi. May Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and the hosts of noble sages, send forth light to receive me and reach down their hands to lift me up. May pavilions, banners, and standards, rare fragrances and heavenly music, and the holy scenes of the West be shown before my eyes. May all beings who see or hear of it rejoice and sigh in admiration and give rise to the bodhi mind.]

When the time of death approaches, may I know the hour in advance. May my body be free of all sickness, suffering, and calamity, and my mind free of all attachment and confusion. May my faculties be joyful and my right mindfulness clear. May I relinquish my karmic-reward body (this flesh body) with inner peace, as if entering samadhi. May Amitabha Buddha, together with Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and the hosts of noble sages, send forth light to receive me and reach down their hands to lift me up. Then pavilions, banners, and standards, rare fragrances and heavenly music, and the holy scenes of the West will be clearly shown before my eyes. May the beings who see or hear of these auspicious signs of rebirth rejoice and sigh in admiration, give rise to the bodhi mind, and seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Knowing the hour in advance] Knowing beforehand the time of rebirth. [Sickness and calamity] Disharmony of the four great elements in the body is called "the suffering of sickness"; encountering fire, flood, war, poison, and the like is called "calamity." [Joyful] Joyous, delighted. [Relinquishing the reward] Letting go of the karmic-reward body (the flesh body). [Noble sages] Among the fifty-two stages, the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications, who have cut off only the delusions of view and thought, are called "worthy" (xian); the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds are called "noble" (sheng). [Clearly shown] Plainly displayed.
